paragraphs.text: Only 8 events are documented here, and some locations in this account are approximate.
Babylon, the capital city of Babylonia, has its founding dated to between 3000 BCE and 2001 BCE.
Ammi-Saduqa, a king of Babylon, was born here between 1800 BCE and 1701 BCE.
The Battle of Babylon came in 710 BCE and the Battle of Kish in 703 BCE.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, are dated to between 700 BCE and 601 BCE.
In 693 BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire fought the Elamites at the Battle of Diyala River, and in 691 BCE the Assyrian empire fought rebelling Babylonians, Elamites and others at the Battle of Halule.
In 689 BCE the Assyrian king Sennacherib, having beaten the Elamites, besieged Babylon for up to fifteen months and destroyed it.
In 626 BCE the general Nabopolassar began a revolt, and by 620 BCE he had consolidated control of Babylonia.
The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, dated to 575 BCE, was constructed by order of King Nebuchadnezzar II.
In September 539 BCE Persia won a decisive victory over the Neo-Babylonian Empire at the Battle of Opis, north of Babylon.
After the battle, Persian forces supposedly entered Babylon without further resistance, and Cyrus the Great was proclaimed king of Babylonia.
Hanno the Navigator, a Carthaginian explorer, was born here in the fifth century BCE, and the general Hamilcar Barca around 275 BCE.
During the First Punic War, a Roman army under Marcus Atilius Regulus won the Battle of Adys.
In spring 255 BCE, a Carthaginian army led by Xanthippus defeated Regulus at the Battle of Bagradas.
Hannibal and Hasdrubal, sons of Hamilcar Barca, were born here in 247 BCE and 245 BCE.
The Mercenary War was a mutiny by troops employed by Carthage.
Early in 240 BCE, both sides were routed at the Battle of Utica.
Later in 240 BCE, Hamilcar Barca defeated rebels led by Spendius at the Battle of the Bagradas River.
A Siege of Carthage is recorded in 239 BCE, and in October 238 BCE Hamilcar Barca besieged rebels under Mathos at Tunis.

In 204 BCE a Roman army under Publius Cornelius Scipio began an unsuccessful siege of Utica, and in 203 BCE he fought allied Carthaginian and Numidian armies at the Great Plains and at Utica, both heavy defeats for Carthage.
Terence, the Roman comic playwright, was born here in 185 BCE.
In 149 BCE a large Roman army landed at Utica, and at the Battle of Lake Tunis the Carthaginians launched fire ships that destroyed most of the Roman fleet.
The Siege of Carthage, the main engagement of the Third Punic War, lasted nearly three years, 149 BCE to 146 BCE.
Some locations in this account are approximate.
Only 8 events are documented here, with 59 people and places, and some locations in this account are approximate.
Sophocles was born here in 496 BCE and Pericles in 494 BCE.
In 480 BCE the Achaemenid Empire captured Athens.
It subsequently razed the Acropolis, the Old Temple of Athena, and the Older Parthenon.
One year later, the Greek coalition retook Athens.
Socrates was born here in 470 BCE.
Pericles led Athens as its preeminent orator and statesman roughly from 461 BCE to 429 BCE.
Aristophanes was born here in 445 BCE.
Spartan invasions of Attica ran from 431 BCE to 425 BCE, and the Plague of Athens from 430 BCE to 426 BCE.

cites.label: Spartan invasions of Attica during the Archidamian War

paragraphs.text: The plague killed an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 people, around 25% of the population.
Plato was born here between 429 BCE and 420 BCE.
In 420 BCE an earthquake disrupted the Athenian assembly.
In 404 BCE came the Siege of Athens.
At the Battle of Munichia, exiles under Thrasybulus held a hill in Piraeus, and the defeated Thirty Tyrants fled to Eleusis.
In 403 BCE, at the Battle of Piraeus, a Spartan force narrowly defeated the exiles, and a settlement then allowed the reestablishment of democratic government in Athens.
In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and corrupting the youth and sentenced to death.
The Athenian-Macedonian War ran from 340 BCE to 338 BCE.
Julius Caesar was born here in 100 BCE.
In 88 BCE the consul Sulla led the March on Rome, the first time a general ordered his army to march against the Republic.
In 82 BCE Sulla won the Battle of the Colline Gate at the northeastern end of Rome and secured control of Italy.
Augustus, also known as Octavian, was born here in 63 BCE.
On the Ides of March, 44 BCE, a group of senators assassinated Julius Caesar during a Senate session at the Curia of Pompey in Rome, stabbing him approximately 23 times.
Tiberius was born in Rome in 42 BCE.
The Perusine War, a civil war from 41 BCE to 40 BCE, was fought by Lucius Antonius in support of Mark Antony against Octavian.
In 49 CE the emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome.

cites.label: Claudius' expulsion of Jews from Rome

paragraphs.text: The Great Fire of Rome began in July 64 CE around the Circus Maximus, and nearly three quarters of Rome was destroyed.
In 69 CE, the Year of the Four Emperors, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian ruled in succession amid turmoil in Rome and the provinces.
That year also brought the Siege of the Capitoline Hill and a Battle of Rome.
Construction of the Colosseum in Rome began under the Emperor Vespasian and was completed under his successor Titus.
Some locations in this account are approximate.
This area has 10 documented events, and some locations in this account are approximate.
Prochorus, born here at a date given only as 1 CE to 100 CE, was one of the Seven Deacons chosen to care for the poor of the Christian community in Jerusalem.
Josephus, best known for writing The Jewish War, was born in Jerusalem around 37 CE.
Around 48 to 50 CE came the Council of Jerusalem, the first Christian synod.
In 66 CE riots in Jerusalem became the catalyst of the First Jewish-Roman War, and the Battle of Jerusalem was fought.
In 67 CE, according to Josephus, the Sicarii of Masada raided Ein Gedi and killed 700 of its inhabitants.
In 68 CE came the Zealot Temple Siege and the Battle of the Jordan River.
In 70 CE Roman forces led by Titus besieged Jerusalem, destroyed the Second Temple, and razed the city, the effective end of the First Jewish Revolt.
The Siege of Machaerus followed in 71 CE, and from 72 CE to 73 CE Roman imperial forces took the hilltop fortress of Masada, held by the Sicarii.
Hegesippus, a Christian writer of the early Church, was born here in 107 CE, and the Siege of Betar is dated 132 CE to 135 CE.
Only 8 events and 44 people and places are documented here, and some locations in this account are approximate.
In 617 the Aws and the Khazraj, the dominant tribes of Medina, fought each other at the Yawm al-Buath, the final armed conflict between them before their conversion to Islam.
The Prophet's Mosque, built by Muhammad, is dated here to 622.
The siege of the Banu Qaynuqa, a Jewish tribe expelled by Muhammad for breaking the Constitution of Medina, occurred in April 624.
In 624 Muhammad took 300 men to Buhran, where the Banu Sulaym fled.
On 23 March 625 the early Muslims fought the Quraysh at the Battle of Uhud, north of Medina.
Hasan ibn Ali, a grandson of Muhammad, was born here in 625, and his younger brother Husayn ibn Ali in 626.
In 627, at the Battle of the Trench, the Muslims defended themselves in Medina by digging a trench around their settlement.
In mid-August 632 forces of Caliph Abu Bakr fought rebellious Arab tribes at the Battle of Abraq in the Nejd region.
Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, later the fifth Umayyad caliph, was born here in 646.
In 656 the caliph Uthman ibn Affan was assassinated at the end of a siege upon his house.
On 26 August 683 the Umayyad army of Yazid I fought the rebel defenders of Medina at the Battle of al-Harrah.
Jaafar Al-Sadiq, a Muslim scholar and Imam, was born here in 699.
Some locations in this account are approximate, including all 8 documented events.
Songtsän Gampo, a Tibetan emperor, was born here in 604 CE.
Lhasa, today the capital of Tibet, was founded in 633 CE.
The Potala Palace dates to 637 CE, and Songtsän Gampo moved the capital to it.

In 1240 the Mongol general Doorda Darkhan invaded Tibet with 30,000 troops, and in the late 1240s Mongol prince Godan invited Sakya Pandita, who urged other leading Tibetan figures to submit to Mongol authority.
Sonam Gyatso, born here in 1543 CE, was later named Dalai Lama by Altan Khan in 1578 for teachings in Mongolia.
Ngawang Lobzang Gyatso, the 5th Dalai Lama, was born here in 1617 CE.
The wars of the Dzungar Khanate against the Qing dynasty, from 1688 CE to 1759 CE, reached Tibet.
In 1720 a Qing expedition took Tibet from the Dzungar Khanate and established Qing rule.
The Lhasa riot of 1750 began after two ambans assassinated Gyurme Namgyal, the expected new regent, and 51 Qing soldiers and 77 Chinese citizens were killed.
In 1788 a dispute over debased silver currency led to a Nepalese invasion of Tibet, followed by the Treaty of Kerung (1789).
Tibet fought the Kingdom of Jammu from May 1841 to August 1842.
The Nepalese-Tibetan War of 1855 to 1856 was fought in Tibet and ended with the Treaty of Thapathali.
In 1910 Qing China sent 2,000 troops to Tibet, causing the Dalai Lama to flee to British India.
Only 8 events are documented here, along with 55 people and places, and some locations in this account are approximate.
Baghdad was founded in 762 CE.
The jurist Ahmad ibn Hanbal was born here in 780 CE and the future caliph al-Ma'mun in 786 CE.
The siege of Baghdad, part of a civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma'mun for the Abbasid Caliphate, lasted from August 812 until September 813.
Al-Ma'mun reigned from 813 until 833 and promoted the flowering of learning and the sciences in Baghdad.
The traveller Ahmad ibn Fadlan was born here in 879 CE and the historian Al-Mas'udi around 896 CE.
A battle of Baghdad is recorded in 932 CE, with no further detail.
In 942 CE the Hamdanids defeated the Baridis near al-Mada'in in a four-day battle for control over Baghdad.
In 946 CE the Buyids under Mu'izz al-Dawla expelled the Hamdanids from Baghdad after months of fighting within the city.
Seljuk forces blockaded the Abbasid capital for fifty days in 1136 CE and besieged it again in 1157 CE, when Caliph al-Muqtafi successfully defended it.
In 1258 CE a Mongol army under Hulegu took and sacked Baghdad, and the caliph al-Musta'sim was killed alongside hundreds of thousands of his subjects.
A sédition de Karkh is also recorded in 1258 CE, with no further detail.
This area has 10 documented events, and some locations in this account are approximate.
The exact date of the founding of Tenochtitlan, on an island in Lake Texcoco, is unclear, but 1325 was later chosen to celebrate its anniversary.
Moctezuma I, born here in 1398, later became the fifth king of Tenochtitlan.
The Mexico Flood of 1446 is documented here.
Moctezuma II, born here in 1466, later became the ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire.
In 1473 Tenochtitlan fought the Battle of Tlatelolco against Tlatelolco, its neighbour on the island.
On 19 February 1475 an earthquake struck Tenochtitlan during the reign of Tlatoani Axayacatl.
Cuauhtémoc, born here in 1495, later became the last Aztec Emperor.
A smallpox epidemic in Tenochtitlan lasted from 1519 to 1520.
On 22 May 1520, during the Spanish conquest, the Feast of Toxcatl ended in a massacre of Mexica elites.

cites.label: Massacre in the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan

paragraphs.text: On 30 June 1521 the Mexica won the Battle of Colhuacatonco, regarded as their most important victory of the siege of Tenochtitlan.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 to the Spanish and thousands of indigenous allies, especially Tlaxcaltec warriors.
The cocoliztli epidemic of 1545 to 1548 brought high fevers and bleeding.
The Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral, dated to 1570, sits on the former Aztec sacred precinct.
The Francisco Hernández expedition ran from 1570 to 1577, and a cocoliztli epidemic lasted from 1576 to 1577.
Only 10 events are documented here, along with 49 people and places, and some locations in this account are approximate.
Seoul was founded in 1395.
Sejong the Great, creator of Hangul, was born here in 1397, and Yi Sun-sin, a Korean admiral, in 1545.
The Imjin War, two Japanese invasions of Korea, ran from 1592 CE to 1598 CE and ended with the withdrawal of Japanese forces after a military stalemate in Korea's southern provinces.
Gojong of the Korean Empire was born here in 1852.
In 1882 soldiers of the Joseon Army began the Imo Incident, an uprising in Seoul.
Korea negotiated treaties with the United Kingdom in 1883, Russia in 1884 and Japan in 1885.
The Donghak Peasant Revolution took place in Korea from 1894 CE to 1895 CE.
On 23 July 1894, during its ceasefire, Imperial Japanese forces occupied Gyeongbokgung palace to establish a pro-Japanese government.
On 8 October 1895, Queen Min, the consort of Gojong, was assassinated by Japanese agents at the royal palace Gyeongbokgung in Seoul.
The Eulsa Treaty of 1905 made Korea a protectorate of Imperial Japan.
On August 1, 1907, in reaction to its disbandment, the Korean army rebelled against Japanese forces at the Namdaemun Gate in Seoul and was suppressed.
The siege of Constantinople from 1394 to 1402 was a long blockade of the capital of the Byzantine Empire by the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I.
Andronikos V Palaiologos was born here in 1400, and Konstantinos XI Palaiologos in 1404.
In 1411, Constantinople was besieged during the Ottoman Interregnum, which followed the defeat of Bayezid I by Timur.
Wikidata records a Byzantine-Ottoman war from 1421 to 1424.
In 1422, the Ottoman Empire laid siege to Constantinople as a result of the Byzantine Emperor Manuel II's attempts to interfere in the succession of Ottoman Sultans.
Konstantinos XI Palaiologos, the last Byzantine emperor, died in battle at the fall of Constantinople on 29 May 1453.
Wikidata dates the founding of Istanbul here to 1453.
On April 18, 1454, the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice signed the Treaty of Constantinople, the first treaty signed by Mehmed the Conqueror after the capture of the city.
The Grand Bazaar dates here to 1455 and Topkapı Palace to 1460, and from the 1460s the palace served as the administrative center of the Ottoman Empire.
In 1479 another Treaty of Constantinople ended the sixteen-year-long war between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire, and Wikidata records a treaty of the same name in 1482.
The Synod of Constantinople in 1484 was the first synod to condemn the Council of Florence.
Some locations in this account are approximate.
The semi-legendary Inca-Chanka war between Cusco and the Chanka chiefdom is dated 1401 CE to 1500 CE.
A Battle of Cusco is recorded in 1438.
Túpac Inca Yupanqui was born here in 1441, Manco Inca in 1500, and Túpac Huallpa in 1510.
In 1533 a Battle of Cusco was fought between the Spanish Conquistadors and forces of the Incas, and battles at Anta and Capi date to that year.
In 1536 Manco Inca Yupanqui led an Incan army in a 10-month siege of Cusco, held by Spanish conquistadors and Indian auxiliaries under Hernando Pizarro.
Sacsayhuaman and Yucay saw battles in 1536.
In 1537 Hernando Pizarro led the besieged in a raid on the emperor's headquarters at Ollantaytambo.
The Incans hoped the siege would restore their empire, but it was ultimately unsuccessful.
In 1538 Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro fought rival conquistador Diego de Almagro at the Battle of Las Salinas.
Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, later a chronicler, was born here in 1539.
In 1548 Gonzalo Pizarro and Pedro de la Gasca fought the Battle of Jaquijahuana, during the Revolt of the Encomenderos.
The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire ended in Spanish victory in 1572 and colonization of the region as the Viceroyalty of Peru.

cites.label: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

This account draws on the most notable of the 27 documented events here.
Some locations in this account are approximate.
Ginkaku-ji, a Zen temple in Kyoto's Sakyo ward, is dated to 1465.
The Ōnin War, a civil war from 1467 to 1477, grew from a dispute between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen.
The Battle of Goryō is recorded here in 1467.
After that war weakened the Ashikaga shogunate, local samurai and peasants in Yamashiro Province rose up in 1485 and demanded the withdrawal of two rival warlord armies.
Their league operated until 1493, when a new invasion forced its members to reaccept the shogunate's authority.
The Eiroku Incident was a 1565 battle, and the Battle of Yasugawara is recorded in 1570.
In 1571 Oda Nobunaga fought the sōhei of Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei near Kyoto.
The Siege of Makishima Castle was a 1573 battle.
In 1582 Nobunaga died by seppuku at Honnō-ji in Kyoto in the rebellion of his vassal Akechi Mitsuhide.
The Battle of Yamazaki, between the forces of Akechi Mitsuhide and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, was fought in 1582.
Emperor Go-Mizunoo was born here in 1596.
In 1600 Fushimi Castle, defended by Torii Mototada for Tokugawa Ieyasu, fell in a battle leading up to the decisive Battle of Sekigahara.
That year Kyōgoku Takatsugu held Ōtsu castle for the Tokugawa.
Empress Meishō was born here in 1624, Go-Kōmyō in 1633 and Go-Sai in 1638.
Only 5 events and 2 people and places are documented here, so this account is short, and 4 of the 5 events have approximate locations.
In 1505, Portuguese forces under the first Viceroy of India, Dom Francisco de Almeida, fought the Sultanate of Mombasa, staged a landing and sacked the city.
In 1528, Portuguese forces under Nuno da Cunha, the Portuguese governor of India, fought the Sultanate of Mombasa.
On 5 March 1589, Portuguese and Zimba forces under Tomé Coutinho fought the Ottomans, and the Portuguese reconquered the city and captured Mir Ali Beg.
Fort Jesus, designed by the Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati, was built on Mombasa Island between 1593 and 1596 by order of King Felipe II of Spain to guard the Old Port of Mombasa.
It was the only fort maintained by the Portuguese on the Swahili coast.
From 13 March 1696 to 13 December 1698, the army of the Ya'rubid ruler of Oman, Saif I bin Sultan, besieged the Portuguese city of Mombasa and Fort Jesus.
In 1899, a famine struck central Kenya around Mount Kenya.
Only 3 events and 1 place are documented here, so this account is short.
The First Battle of Panipat, on 21 April 1526, was fought between the invading forces of Babur and Ibrahim Khan Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi.
Babur's forces, employing gunpowder firearms and cannons, defeated Ibrahim in one of the earliest battles involving gunpowder arms on the Indian subcontinent.
The victory marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India.
The Kabuli Bagh Mosque in Panipat was built in 1527 by the emperor Babur to mark that victory, and it is named after Kabuli Begum, Babur's wife.

cites.label: Kabuli Bagh Mosque with enclosure wall

paragraphs.text: The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on 5 November 1556, between the Mughals under Akbar and king Hemu, titularly known as Hemchandra Vikramaditya.
A few weeks earlier, Hemchandra had conquered Delhi and Agra by defeating Mughal forces under Tardi Beg Khan in the Battle of Delhi.
The Third Battle of Panipat took place on 14 January 1761, in and around the city of Panipat, between the Maratha Empire and the invading army of the Durrani Empire.
The Afghans were supported by three key allies in India: Najib-ud-Daula, elements of the declining Mughal Empire, and the Oudh State under Shuja-ud-Daula.
The Maratha army was led by Sadashivrao Bhau, third-highest authority of the Maratha Confederacy after the Chhatrapati and the Peshwa.
Only 8 events and 3 people and places are documented here, so this account is short.
Some locations in this account are approximate.
The 1751 Port-au-Prince earthquake occurred on 21 November in Saint-Domingue, followed by a tsunami.
Alexandre Pétion was born here in 1770 and Jean-Pierre Boyer in 1776.
Both later became presidents of Haiti.
The Battle of Croix-des-Bouquets in 1792 and the siege of Port-au-Prince in April 1793 both took place during the Haitian Revolution.
In 1794 came the Battle of Port-Républicain, also during the Haitian Revolution, and the Battle of Trutier.
The Siege of Jacmel, a four-and-half month long siege during the War of the South, ran from 1799 to 1800.
Port-au-Prince was besieged again from October to November 1803, also during the Haitian Revolution.
Fort Dimanche, a fortress near La Saline in Port-au-Prince, dates from 1804.
In 1807 came the Battle of Sibert.

Some locations in this account are approximate.
On 17 July 1791, the Champ de Mars Massacre struck a crowd of republican protesters in Paris.
On 10 August 1792, armed revolutionaries stormed the Tuileries Palace, leading France to abolish the monarchy and establish a republic.
The Louvre Museum is dated here to 1793.
The Revolt of 1 Prairial Year III, on 20 May 1795, was the final major popular uprising of the French Revolution.
In 1795, 13 Vendémiaire, a battle in the streets of Paris, advanced the career of Napoleon Bonaparte.
In 1797, the Coup of 18 Fructidor ousted the monarchists from the legislature.
Eugène Delacroix was born here in 1798.
On 9 November 1799, the bloodless Coup of 18 Brumaire overthrew the Directory and brought Napoleon Bonaparte to power as First Consul.
Napoleon Bonaparte and Pope Pius VII signed the Concordat of 1801 in Paris on 15 July 1801.
Napoleon was crowned Emperor of the French on December 2, 1804, at Notre-Dame de Paris.
George Sand was born here in 1804, Alexis de Tocqueville in 1805, and Napoleon III in 1808.
Bernard Courtois discovered iodine in 1811.
In 1814, Allied forces drove back the defenders of Paris, and the French evacuated it on 31 March.
The Treaty of Paris was signed on 30 May 1814 and the Second Treaty of Paris on 20 November 1815.
On 22 January 1879, eleven days after the British invaded the Zulu Kingdom, a Zulu force of some 20,000 warriors attacked a portion of the British main column at Isandlwana.
During the final hours of the British defeat there, a large contingent of Zulu warriors broke off and travelled ten kilometres to attack the mission station at Rorke's Drift.
A vastly outnumbered British force under Lieutenants John Chard and Gonville Bromhead held it, and the battle holds the record for the most Victoria Crosses awarded for a single battle.
Hattingspruit, a coal mining town, was established here in the 1880s.

The Battle of Talana Hill, in 1899, was the first major clash of the Second Boer War, and the Battle of Elandslaagte, fought while the Boers were invading Natal, was one of the few decisive British victories.
On 30 October 1899 a British sortie from Ladysmith ended in disaster, and the Boers began a siege of the town on 2 November 1899.
Redvers Buller's attempts to relieve it started on 15 December 1899 at the Second Battle of Colenso, where the Boers repelled British forces on the Tugela River.
The Battle of Vaal Krantz, in 1900, was his third failed attempt to fight past Louis Botha's Boer army.
From 14 February to 27 February 1900, at the Battle of the Tugela Heights, Buller's army forced Botha's army to lift the siege, which lasted until 28 February 1900.
This area has 18 documented events; 12 are told here, and some locations are approximate.
In 1900 Boxers and Qing Dynasty troops besieged the foreign legations in Peking for 55 days, until the Eight-Nation Alliance relieved them.
Only the Treaty of Peking's name and year, 1905, are documented here.
Puyi, the last Qing emperor, was born here in 1906.
In 1917 Zhang Xun's army seized Beijing and reinstalled Puyi, a restoration Republican troops reversed within two weeks.
On May 4, 1919, students protested at Tiananmen, beginning the May Fourth Movement.
Feng Yuxiang staged the Beijing Coup in 1924, students in Beiping demanded resistance to Japanese aggression in 1935, and in 1937 battles near Beiping and Tianjin ended in a Japanese victory.
Xi Jinping was born here in 1953, Ai Weiwei in 1957, and Jet Li in 1963.
Red August, beginning in August 1966 during the Cultural Revolution, was a period of political violence and massacres in Beijing.
In April 1976, after Zhou Enlai's death, crowds protested at Tiananmen Square, and that October a bloodless coup arrested the Gang of Four.
Zhang Ziyi was born here in 1979.
Official statistics published in 1980 said Red Guards killed 1,772 during Red August; those of November 1985 gave 10,275 deaths.

From 15 April to 4 June 1989, protests led by students and workers were held in Tiananmen Square; on the night of 3 June the Chinese government deployed troops to occupy the square in what is referred to as the Tiananmen Square massacre.
Of the 23 documented events here, this account follows 12 of them.
The Gallipoli campaign, a First World War campaign on the Gallipoli Peninsula, began on 19 February 1915.
In 1915, Royal Navy, French, Russian and Australian ships attempted to force a passage through the Dardanelles Straits; the placement of these operations is approximate.

cites.label: naval operations in the Dardanelles Campaign

paragraphs.text: On 25 April 1915, amphibious landings by British and French forces included Cape Helles, and British Empire forces landed at Anzac Cove, beginning the campaign's land phase.
The First Battle of Krithia, from 28 April, was the first Allied attempt to advance, and Ottoman forces quickly overwhelmed it.
In the Second Battle of Krithia, the Allies captured only a small amount of ground after two days of costly fighting.
In August 1915 the British made their final attempt to seize the peninsula, the August Offensive or Battle of Sari Bair.
The landing at Suvla Bay, part of that offensive, began on the night of 6 August 1915.
Between 6 and 10 August, ANZAC and Ottoman forces fought at Lone Pine in a diversionary attack.
On 7 August the minor Battle of the Nek took place on a narrow ridge that was easy to defend.
The Battle of Hill 60, launched on 21 August, was one of the last major assaults of the campaign.
The campaign lasted until 9 January 1916, and the Allied attempt to control the Turkish straits failed.
Later, on 20 January 1918, an Ottoman squadron engaged a Royal Navy flotilla off Imbros.
